extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners (and patent practitioners preparing/responding to written description issues)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent application’s specification adequately supports claimed subject matter under 35 U.S.C. 112 (written description requirement). Covers claim-by-claim analysis, evidence of possession, means-plus-function issues, and factors tied to the art and technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: For Each Claim, Determine What the Claim as a Whole Covers
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction is an essential part of the examination. Each claim must be separately analyzed and given its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entire claim must be considered including preamble language and the transitional phrase. Consider whether preamble recitations constitute structural limitations by review of the entire application. Apply broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification. See In re Katz; Pac-Tec; Bell Communications; Corning Glass Works; Lockwood. Limitations may not be imported into the claims from the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of Transitional Phrases ('comprising', 'consisting essentially of', 'consisting of')
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Comprising' is open-ended (covers recited subject matter alone or in combination with unrecited subject matter). 'Consisting essentially of' signals inclusion of listed ingredients and exclusion of unlisted ingredients that materially affect basic and novel properties; absent clear specification, it will be construed equivalent to 'comprising' for 102/103 purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant bears burden to show that additional steps/materials are excluded by 'consisting essentially of' by proving material change. See Genentech v. Chiron; Ex parte Davis; PPG Indus.; AK Steel; In re Janakirama-Rao; In re De Lajarte; MPEP § 2111.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review the Entire Application to Understand Support for Claimed Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Before determining written description sufficiency, review claims and the entire specification (including embodiments, figures, sequence listings) to understand how applicant provides support for claim features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine field of invention and level of skill in the art. For some arts there is an inverse correlation between skill level and specificity required. Information well known in the art need not be described in detail. See Rasmussen; Amgen v. Chugai; Wang Labs.; Hybritech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written Description Requirement: Applicant Must Show Possession of the Claimed Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be sufficient written description to inform a skilled artisan that the applicant was in possession of the claimed invention as a whole at filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a factual, case-by-case inquiry. The description must demonstrate possession of the claimed invention with all its limitations. See Purdue Pharma; Pfaff v. Wells; Lockwood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession Shown by Actual Reduction to Practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession may be shown by describing an actual reduction to practice: the inventor constructed an embodiment or performed a process that met all limitations and determined the invention would work for its intended purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction to practice provides strong evidence of possession but is not always necessary. See Cooper v. Goldfarb; UMC Elecs.; Estee Lauder; Mahurkar. For biological materials, deposits per 37 CFR 1.801 et seq. (esp. 1.804, 1.809) can evidence reduction to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession Shown by Detailed Drawings or Structural Chemical Formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings or structural chemical formulas that are sufficiently detailed may show applicant was in possession of the claimed invention as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings alone may provide a written description. See Vas-Cath; In re Wolfensperger; Autogiro; Eli Lilly. Use of generic formulae can indicate what genus claims encompass in chemical arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession Shown by Sufficient Identifying Characteristics (function, structure, properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of sufficiently detailed, relevant identifying characteristics—such as partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics coupled with known correlation to structure, sequence, binding affinity, specificity, molecular weight, length—can demonstrate possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the art has established a strong correlation between structure and function, minimal structural disclosure plus function may suffice. Examples: antibodies where antigen is fully characterized and generation is routine. See Enzo Biochem; Falkner; Capon v. Eshhar; Centocor; Noelle v. Lederman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function-Only Definitions Do Not Suffice Without Structure-Function Correlation
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition by function alone does not satisfy the written description requirement unless there is a well-established correlation between function and structure permitting prediction of structure from function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure of function without means to identify structure is 'little more than a wish' and inadequate. See Eli Lilly; In re Wilder; Fiers; Amgen v. Chugai.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means- (or Step-) Plus-Function Limitations (35 U.S.C. 112(f)/pre-AIA §112, para.6) Must Have Corresponding Structure/Materials/Acts in Specification
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (or pre-AIA para. 6), it must be interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, materials, or acts disclosed in the specification and 'equivalents thereof.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The written description must adequately link particular structure/materials/acts to perform the recited function, or make it clear one skilled in the art would know the corresponding structure. Reliance on a skilled artisan's ability to implement is insufficient without disclosure. See B. Braun; Aristocrat; Atmel; Biomedino. A 112(b) indefiniteness rejection for lack of corresponding structure often requires a simultaneous 112(a) written description rejection. See In re Noll; MPEP § 2181; Supplemental Examination Guidelines (65 Fed. Reg. 38510).

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-Known or Conventional Information Need Not Be Disclosed in Detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Information which is well known in the art need not be described in detail in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply knowledge of the art to balance what must be disclosed. The written description requirement is applied in context of the particular invention and state of knowledge; as fields evolve, the balance between known information and inventive contribution evolves. See Hybritech; Capon v. Eshhar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species vs Genus Analysis (Single Embodiment/Species vs Genus Claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limited to a single disclosed embodiment or species is analyzed as a species; a claim encompassing two or more embodiments/species is analyzed as a genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each claim drawn to a single embodiment/species: (A) determine whether application describes an actual reduction to practice; (B) if not, determine whether reduction to drawings or structural chemical formulas sufficiently detailed to show possession; (C) if not, determine whether invention is described with distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficiently detailed to show possession. Then (1) does the application describe the complete structure or acts of the process? If yes, written description satisfied; (2) if not, are there other relevant identifying characteristics (function+structure correlation) sufficient to demonstrate possession? See MPEP § 806.04(e) and cases cited (Fields v. Conover; others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to Consider in Determining Written Description Sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether specification shows applicant was in possession is a factual determination considering multiple factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics (esp. with known structure-function correlation), method of making the claimed invention. Also rely on patents/printed publications to assess maturity of the art. See Eli Lilly; Capon v. Eshhar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological Maturity and Predictability Affect Required Disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: In mature, predictable arts, less detailed disclosure may be sufficient; in emerging or unpredictable technologies, more evidence is required to show possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In mature technologies with high skill/knowledge, written description questions are less likely for originally filed claims even if specification shows only method of making and function. In unpredictable/emerging fields, disclosure of only method+function may not support a product claim (except product-by-process if process actually used to produce the product). Partial structure without further characterization may be insufficient. See Amgen; Fiers v. Revel; discussion of product-by-process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure Must Distinguish the Claimed Invention from Other Materials
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must provide identifying characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention from other materials and lead a skilled artisan to conclude applicant was in possession of the claimed species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure of any combination of identifying characteristics (structure, properties, function with correlation, method of making) that allows distinction can be sufficient. See Eli Lilly; Lockwood; cases on biochemical identifiers and enzymatic properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection Guidance: Adequate Description Precludes 112(a) Rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: If a complete structure is disclosed for a species/embodiment, the written description requirement is satisfied and a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) must not be made for lack of written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification discloses complete structure (or acts of a process) of the claimed invention as a whole, do not make 112(a) rejection. See Fields v. Conover and accompanying MPEP instructions.
